A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the changed title and terminology. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original phase-retrieval and distributionally robust optimization experiments, including algorithm comparisons and parameter sweeps in Figures 2–3.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained problems, CIFAR10 neural-network training, and extensive ablations in Section 7 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The independent sampling, power normalization, and clipping mechanisms are retained. However, v1 Equation 13's fixed gradient multiplier 2 and scale (4L1γ)^(1/β) become adjustable A and Γ in v2 Equation 14, with revised noise-dependent prescriptions in Theorem 2. This is a limited normalization-calibration change; the NGD/AN-GD and I-NSGD/IAN-SGD renamings alone are not counted.

E1.justification: v2 adds training ResNet18 and ResNet50 on CIFAR10, substantially extending coverage to image-classification neural-network optimization. The synthetic phase-retrieval problem and life-expectancy DRO task remain.

E2.justification: v1 compares against SGD, normalized SGD, and clipped SGD. v2 adds SPIDER and normalized SGD with momentum to the retained phase-retrieval and DRO comparisons, as confirmed by Figure 2. The new neural-network comparisons also evaluate Adam and Adagrad.

E3.justification: Settings change substantially on retained tasks: phase retrieval changes the independent batch size from 8 to 4 and the proposed method's learning rate from 0.5 to 0.25; DRO changes these from 16 to 8 and 0.28 to 0.11. Clipping and stabilization parameters also change. New experiments introduce shared-normalization controls and small-batch protocols. The neural-network budget is internally unclear: Section 7.3 states 30 epochs, while Figure 3 extends to 60 and 80.

E4.justification: v1 already studies normalization power and independent batch size. v2 retains and revises these analyses, then adds comparisons with normalization power unified across baselines, stabilization-parameter sensitivity, noise-coefficient sensitivity, and joint batch-size sweeps down to one sample. Appendix A.4 also compares algorithms under small batches on all three application types.

E5.justification: v2 Section 7.3 newly states that a random seed is fixed before neural-network initialization. Neither version documents repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is added seed information, not evidence of increased replication.

E6.justification: v2 adds neural-network loss curves and numerous normalization, stabilization, noise, and small-batch results. The retained benchmark curves are revised under changed settings, so they do not establish same-setting performance gains over v1. Notably, the new shared-normalization comparison in Figure 4, left, shows clipped SGD reaching low loss before IAN-SGD.

T1.justification: v2 restricts the PŁ exponent from ρ > 0 to 0 < ρ ≤ 2 and the multiplicative-noise coefficient to 0 ≤ τ1 < 1. It replaces v1 Appendix E's pointwise mini-batch noise bound with new triangle-inequality bounds, revises Theorem 1's complexity expressions, and adds Proposition 1 comparing GD plus a phase-retrieval smoothness proof. v1's stochastic PŁ Theorem 3 is replaced by a modified descent lemma and revised rate discussion in Section 6.3.2 and Appendix J.

C1.justification: The central contributions—deterministic normalization analysis and O(ε^-4) stochastic optimization with constant-level batches—remain. v2 explicitly strengthens the deterministic contribution into a claim about normalization's advantage over GD, while the stochastic guarantee is scoped to the newly restricted multiplicative-noise range.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation connecting GD's slow convergence to its gradient-bound-dependent learning rate, and describes clipping as recovering SGD behavior near stationarity. It also adds practical failure conditions and recommendations concerning small normalization powers, excessive learning rates, and batch sizes. Appendix A introduces further interpretations of stabilization and noise sensitivity beyond v1's existing normalization and sampling discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds neural-network preprocessing, Kaiming initialization, PyTorch optimizer implementation information, SPIDER refresh settings, and extensive ablation hyperparameters. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix H.1's detailed DRO imputation, feature processing, training-subset selection, target-noise injection, and initialization instructions. Their disappearance establishes lost documentation, not that the underlying data pipeline changed.

R1.justification: v2 expands research positioning through Table 1's comparison of noise assumptions, batch requirements, and convergence guarantees, detailed clipping-method comparisons, and connections to KŁ geometry. It acknowledges concurrent independent-sampling work by Vankov et al. and adds works including Cutkosky and Mehta, Koloskova et al., and Li and Pong. The earlier Karimi et al. citation is removed.

P1.justification: The title, method terminology, introduction, and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten. Related work, notation, and generalized-smoothness background become separate sections. Existing ablations move into the first appendix, while the stochastic PŁ analysis receives a main-text subsection and a reorganized appendix treatment. These are extensive narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and title/author layout. v1's phase-retrieval and DRO triptychs are reorganized into paired benchmark plots and separate appendix sweeps. v2 also adds the literature-comparison table and neural-network, normalization-control, stabilization, noise, and small-batch figures. The retained bias illustration is relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important analytical deficiency by replacing v1's unsupported pointwise 1/sqrt(B) noise-reduction step with a directly justified bound under an explicit, narrower noise assumption. Expanded baselines and shared-normalization controls substantially improve the assessment of the method's advantage, including cases favoring clipped SGD. These gains outweigh the loss of DRO preprocessing details and the inconsistent neural-network epoch reporting, although those issues limit reproducibility.
